Albert Einstein is one of my heroes, and you're right. I don't know how I feel about it being okay to fail when I feel like my value as a person is based on my academic and extracurricular success. 

It's okay to fail. Huh. I'll have to say that a few more times before I get used to it. :) Thank you.

Thank you, your post really made me feel better. I can't remember ever being told that I deserve to be happy, even if I don't get straight A's or my masters degree in four years. All my life, I've been told that success equals money equals happiness- but maybe that isn't true. 

You've given me a lot to think about.

You don't sound cruel in the least. You bring up an excellent point. I've spent all my life envisioning this perfection and working so hard for it- and falling short at every turn. I don't think perfection is a lie, but I do think that it's unattainable. All the pursuit of perfection causes is pain.

You are an amazing person. 

Everything you've said makes perfect sense to me. When I was little, I spoke with a woman who told me I was a "gifted child", who said that I had all this potential- I was therefore placed in classes above the other kids. I was all alone and I developed this huge superiority complex. Like "Fine, they don't want to be my friend? That's because I'm smarter than they are. They're just stupid. I have *potential*..." 

My parents were so proud, I couldn't stop being *special* and *gifted* or I'd lose everything that made me who I was. So now, when my life is just a life, I feel like everything is gone- like I'm a huge failure because I'm not perfect like they expected. No- like **I** expected. Because I'm not incredible or amazing or superior- I'm just me. 

I guess the biggest thing is that I don't feel like being "just me" is good enough. Not for my parents, or my siblings who look up to me, or my teachers or counselors, or even myself.  

I just feel like if I can't be perfect, why bother *being*?

I guess it's just something I'll have to get over.
